event_description: State of Emergency (Eastern Washington) — GOVERNOR 14-04 WHEREAS, the month of July 2014 has been extremely dry, there are multiple ongoing wildfires throughout Eastern Washington, and current and projected weather conditions, in conjunction with existing and projected fire fuel conditions, present a continuing high risk of severe wildfires throughout all counties of Eastern Washington State
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The largest fire in Washington State history is now the 2014 Carlton Complex.  Central Washington was in drought status.  The fire was started by lightning on July 14.  The complex started as four fires; the Stokes Fire, The Gold Hikes Fire, the French Creek Fire, and the Cougar Flat Fire.  Explosive fire activity occurred on July 16th with very hot, dry, and unstable conditions in place.  Each fire then made runs over the ridgetops and grew into one fire between July 17th and July 18th as hot and windy conditions developed.  The fire rapidly spread through the communities of Methow, Pateros, Carlton, and Olema, and portions of Brewster consuming approximately 325 homes, barns, outbuildings and fences, utilities, cattle and livestock, and orchards, crops, forest, and range land in its path.  The fire burned 269,186 acres consisting of a combination of brush, timber and heavy fuels.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The lightning-caused fire, which began July 14, blackened 269,186 acres; leveled approximately 325 homes; 146 barns, outbuildings and fences; damaged utilities; killed cattle, wildlife and other stock; and destroyed or damaged orchards, crops, forest and range land. Total cost to fight the fire was approximately 87 million dollars.  The fire spanned two different public zones and cost and acreage is highly uncertain per zone.

event_description: State of Emergency (Eastern Washington) — GOVERNOR 14-04 WHEREAS, the month of July 2014 has been extremely dry, there are multiple ongoing wildfires throughout Eastern Washington, and current and projected weather conditions, in conjunction with existing and projected fire fuel conditions, present a continuing high risk of severe wildfires throughout all counties of Eastern Washington State
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Chiwaukum Complex was seven fires spread across Chelan County between Lake Chelan and the Highway 2 corridor.  The complex consisted of the Chiwaukum Creek, Shoofly, Mills Canyon, Kelly Mountain, Alpine Fire, Duncan, and Hansel Creek.  The fires were started on July 15th at approximately 0600 PST from lightning.  Hot and dry conditions on the 16th followed by hot and windy conditions on the 17th and 18th helped the fires spread rapidly.  Steep terrain in the East Slopes of the Cascades also contributed to wildfire growth.  The fire burned through a combination of timber including Ponderosa pine, grand fir, silver fir, mountain hemlock, sub-alpine fir, and slash.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Chiwaukum Complex erupted on July 15th at approximately 0600 PST and was started from a lightning strike on July 14th.  The complex of fires burned 50,540 acres. 543 homes were threatened over the 45 day period but none were lost. Four other structures were burned including one outbuilding and three seasonal cabins. The approximate cost for fighting the fire was 38 million dollars.  The Chiwaukum Creek Fire burned 13,895 acres; Alpine Fire burned 19 acres; Kelly Mountain Fire burned 124 acres; Shoofly Fire burned 163 acres; Mills Canyon Fire burned 22,571 acres; Hansel Creek Fire burned 1,073 acres; Duncan Fire burned 12,695 acres north of Entiat, WA.

event_description: State of Emergency (Eastern Washington) — GOVERNOR 14-04 WHEREAS, the month of July 2014 has been extremely dry, there are multiple ongoing wildfires throughout Eastern Washington, and current and projected weather conditions, in conjunction with existing and projected fire fuel conditions, present a continuing high risk of severe wildfires throughout all counties of Eastern Washington State
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed upper-level low was positioned over Eastern Washington on the afternoon of July 14th.  The cold pool associated with the low combined with surface temperatures in the nineties led to a unstable afternoon air mass and widely scattered thunderstorms.  Precipitable water values were near nine tenths of an inch, the afternoon sounding indicated an inverted V profile, and the presence of the upper-low led to a low shear environment.  Nonetheless, isolated storms became strong producing a combination of heavy rain, small hail, and gusty outflow winds.  Thunderstorm winds knocked down trees in two small areas of Spokane and Okanogan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brush fire on Old Miner Road off Mount Spokane Road burned half an acre and two outbuildings.  The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

event_description: State of Emergency (Okanogan County mudslides) — on July 15, 2014, Proclamation 14-04 was issued proclaiming a state of emergency throughout Eastern Washington due to existing wildfires and the extreme risk of additional wildfires, including the 270,000 acre Carlton Complex wildfire in Okanogan County that continues to burn and has resulted in significant damage to homes, public facilities, and roadway infrastructure
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A downed power line was thought to be responsible for a twenty acre brush fire north of Deer Park near Eloika Lake.  It was not clear what caused the power line to go down.  Multiple outbuildings and vehicles were burned in the blaze.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 20 acre brush fire burned five outbuildings, a camper trailer, a horse trailer, an RV, and a car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Saul Fire is believed to have been started from the same storm system that ignited the Buck Creek Fire (by lightning on July 22,2016), but the Saul Fire was not reported until almost a month later. The difference between how these two fires burned makes for a great example as to how fire spreads in environments that have, or have not, seen recent fire activity. It is believed that the Buck Creek Fire area had not experienced any recent fire activity over the last couple centuries, while the Saul Fire area had seen fire activity over the last couple of decades. The Saul Fire grew to 550 acres (as the most recent fire report of October 6th notes). This fire has yet to be reported as extinguished but is considered inactive (Having likely been controlled sometime during the late summer). The expectation is that winter snowfall will put it out.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated costs associated with mitigation/suppression of the Saul Fire was $7,000.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An above average snow pack in the mountains drained by the Pend Oreille and Clark Fork River basins melted at an accelerated rate during the month of May. Run off from this snow melt caused the Pend Oreille River to achieve moderate flood level for an extended period of time from the middle of May through the first week of June. ||Numerous homes along the river particularly between the towns of Newport and Jared suffered flooding. Inundated yards, recreation sites and first floor flooding of homes and buildings extended as far north as Ione. Water covered portions of Deeter, Sandy Shores, McCloud Creek, Yergens, Bear Paw and Davis Roads, and inundated the Sandy Shores neighborhood near Deeter Road.||Due to the high flow, cold water and debris in the channel, the Pend Oreille Sheriff's office closed the river to all recreation through the end of the month. Pend Oreille County was included in a State of Emergency Declaration by the Washington State Governor for this flooding event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The USGS River Flow Gage at Abeni Falls Dam which controls the flow of the Pend Oreille River surpassed the Flood Flow of 95,000 Cubic Feet per Second (CFS) at 2:30 PM PST on May 11th. The flow increased and passed through the Moderate Flood Flow of 115,000 CFS at 12:15 PM on May 18th. The flow continued to increase and peaked at the  Moderate Flood reading of 121,000 CFS at at 5:00 AM on May 27th. The flow continued to fluctuate between 118,000 CFS and 121,000 CFS through the end of May. The flow receded to below the Flood Flow on June 6th.

event_description: State of Emergency — dangerous fire fuel and weather conditions exist throughout the state of Washington, creating a high risk of severe wildfires igniting and demanding immediate response of firefighting resources to protect people, homes, businesses, and public and private property
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very dry conditions over Eastern Washington during July and August created dry fuel conditions across the region. Scattered dry thunderstorms moving through the region  during the last week of July, caused a number of wildfires some of which grew large and long lasting requiring considerable state and federal resources to contain. These large fires were generally in unpopulated forest land with no structures or homes lost. Smoke from these fires and fires in surrounding states and provinces often severely degraded air quality across eastern Washington during the month of August.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Crescent Mountain Wildfire 20 miles southwest of Twisp was caused by lightning and first detected on July 29th. The fire grew through the month of August eventually consuming 52,609 acres of timber in the upper reaches of the Twisp River Valley before being contained in mid September.  The fire burned in unpopulated wilderness and no structures were lost. The cost of the resources to fight the fire was estimated at 39.4 million dollars.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Pullman Radio reported that the Chief Timothy Wildfire started when a motorhome traveling along the Snake River caught fire. There were no injuries.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Badger Lake, Williams Lake, and Chapman Lake, located 10 miles to the southwest of Cheney, were threatened by numerous wildfires started on August 16th. A total of 333 acres were burned by ignitions started by unknown causes. With many dry fuels, strong winds, and low relative humidity, the Badger Lake fire was not fully contained until August 21st. The three other fires were much smaller and contained shortly after crews arrived. While there were many structures threatened, no known homes or out buildings were lost.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Badger Lake Fire, 10 miles southwest of Cheney, started on August 18 by unknown causes and burned a total 244 acres of timber before contained on August 21. There were Level 3 evacuation notices and approximately 30 structures threatened, but none were damaged or lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 1.3 million dollars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Passing showers on the Waterville Plateau had embedded thunderstorms with a few lightning strikes and gusty winds. With the strong winds, hot conditions and dry fuels fueled the fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Whitehall Road Fire, near Coulee Meadows, started on July 8th and burned a total 800 acres before it was contained on July 10th. The fire was ignited by lightning with a passing evening thunderstorm. Local news reported that gusty winds created blackout conditions from blowing dust and fire spread in many directions. There are no known injuries or property loss. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 300,000 dollars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Red flag conditions, with very low humidity and breezy winds, led to the ideal set up for  wildfire ignition. In addition, the inaccessible terrain, with steep drainages and cliffs, made conditions more difficult to extinguish the fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Batterman Road Fire, in eastern Wenatchee, started on July 4th and burned a total 14,100 acres of brush before it was contained on July 13th. The cause of ignition is unknown and under investigation by authorities. There were no injuries or structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 6.6 million dollars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough Gulf Low continued off the west coast that brought a series of atmospheric rivers resulting in flooding across parts of western Washington. This second atmospheric river episode of the month was a set of three atmospheric rivers back-to-back-to-back. Water vapor transport into Western Washington averaged 160 - 200% of normal during the period of 11 November - 16 November. Heavy rainfall spread across the region on the night of the 11th through November 12, with the heaviest rain starting across Southwest Washington and slowly shifting to the north through the day. Rainfall totals ranged from 5 to 10 inches in spots leading to areal and river flooding, including major flooding. |Heavy, persistent rainfall associated with the Atmospheric River shifted northward across Western Washington on November 13 before stalling over northwest Washington November 14 through 16. Another 5 to 10 inches of rainfall fell across the northern half of western Washington. The snow level rose to 8000 to 10,000 feet, resulting in some snow melt contributing to runoff.  Widespread minor or greater flooding occurred. Major flooding occurred on the Bogachiel, the three forecast points on the Nooksack, Skagit, and Cowlitz Rivers. Moderate flooding occurred on the Elwha, Skokomish, Skykomish, Snohomish, Snoqualmie, Puyallup, Nisqually, Newaukum Rivers and South Prairie Creek. Preliminary record flows occurred on Nooksack, Bogachiel, Calawah Rivers and Olsen Creek. Hundreds of water rescues and two fatalities took place during this time period. The heavy rainfall also triggered numerous landslides due to loading on the already-saturated soils.|Much of the reported damage amounts were for both episodes in November and some of the amounts for this episode were an estimated proportion for the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain on already saturated soils caused several landslides along SR 112, including a large landslide near Sekiu that cutoff the water main to the town. One section of the highway dropped 2 1/2 feet, and other locations were buried in rock, mud, and trees.

event_description: December Atmospheric River and Winter Weather Event, Emergency Assistance, and Truck Driver Hours Waiver
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An atmospheric river brought heavy rains to the Cascades December 8 through 10. The East slopes saw 48 hour rain amounts of up to 7 inches along the crest, 3 to 4 inches in the mid slopes, and at least half an inch in the low land areas. The rain combined with snow melt and led to several flooding and landslide incidents. The flooding forced the closure of highway US 2 for several weeks. An embedded cold front brought high winds in the 60 mph range to the region causing downed trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of trees downed by wind in Chelan County. NWS Survey reported numerous snapped trees observed off of Mountain Home Road. Gusts of 77 to 82 mph on Tumwater Mountain weather sensor were recorded northwest of Leavenworth at 1600 LST. A trained spotter reported numerous trees down across powerlines. Blewett Pass was closed from 1800 Dec 10 to 1500 Dec 11 due to trees across US 97. Damage is estimated.
